questions.stem: How many bones form the cranium?
questions.why: The cranium, also called the neurocranium, comprises 8 bones. The skull as a whole totals 28.

options.why: That is the total number of skull bones.
That overstates the cranial count.
That is closer to the whole skull.

questions.stem: Besides the forehead, what does the frontal bone form?
questions.why: The frontal bone forms the forehead and the superior part of each eye's orbit.

options.t: The lateral wall of each orbit
options.why: The lateral walls come from other bones.

options.t: The back wall of the skull
options.why: That is the occipital bone.

options.t: The superior part of each orbit
The floor of the cranial cavity
options.why: The sphenoid forms much of that floor.

questions.stem: Which part of the cranium do the parietal bones form?
questions.why: The paired parietal bones form most of the superior and lateral walls of the cranium and meet at the sagittal suture.

options.t: The floor of the cranial cavity
options.why: The sphenoid contributes to that floor.

options.t: The posterior base of the skull
options.why: That is the occipital bone.
That is the frontal bone.

options.t: Most of the top and side walls

questions.stem: When does the fontanel formed by the parietal bones begin to close?
questions.why: The fontanel formed by the parietal bones starts to close between 7 and 18 months.

options.why: That is later than the stated window.
That is earlier than the stated window.
It stays open to allow skull growth.

questions.stem: What attaches to the styloid process?
questions.why: The styloid process is a sharp, needlelike projection of the temporal bone used as an attachment point by several neck muscles.

options.why: Those attach elsewhere on the mandible and temporal bone.
Those anchor mainly to the hyoid.
That attaches to the temporal fossa.

questions.stem: The zygomatic process of the temporal bone joins which bone?
questions.why: The zygomatic process is a thin bridge of bone joining the cheekbone, or zygomatic bone.

options.why: The nasal bone forms the bridge of the nose.
The maxilla forms the upper jaw.
The mandible articulates at a different joint.

questions.stem: Where is the mastoid process located?
questions.why: The mastoid process sits behind and below the external bony ear canal and provides an attachment site for some neck muscles.

options.t: At the base of the occipital bone
options.why: That is where the occipital condyles sit.

options.t: Behind and below the ear canal
Above the orbit on the frontal bone
options.why: That is the supraorbital region.

options.t: Directly in front of the ear canal
options.why: That area holds the temporomandibular joint.

questions.stem: Why is a middle ear infection dangerous near the mastoid?
questions.why: The mastoid process is composed of air cavities forming the mastoid sinuses of the middle ear. Their closeness to the brain means infection can spread and cause meningitis.

options.t: It drains into the internal jugular vein
options.why: Venous drainage is not the stated concern.

options.t: Its air cavities sit close to the brain
It is directly open to the environment
options.why: It is not open to the outside.

options.t: It has no blood supply or immune defense
options.why: The area is well vascularized.

questions.stem: Which part of the skull does the occipital bone form?
questions.why: The occipital bone is the most posterior bone of the cranium, forming the base and back wall of the skull.

options.why: That is formed by the parietal bones.

options.t: The lateral walls below the parietals
options.why: The temporal bones form much of that.
The sphenoid and frontal contribute there.

questions.stem: What passes through the foramen magnum?
questions.why: The foramen magnum is the large opening at the base of the occipital bone. It surrounds the lower brainstem and lets the spinal cord connect with the brain.

options.why: That passes through the mental foramen.
That passes through the optic canal.
That enters through a separate canal.

questions.stem: Why does the foramen magnum matter in rising intracranial pressure?
questions.why: The foramen magnum is the only place the brain can swell, which is exactly what herniation is — the reason a fixed cranial vault makes rising pressure so lethal.

options.why: Those sit in the brainstem itself.

options.t: It is the only place the brain can swell
It is where cerebrospinal fluid is produced
options.why: CSF is made in the ventricles.

options.t: It is where the vertebral arteries enter
options.why: Vessel entry is not what makes it dangerous.

questions.stem: What do the occipital condyles rest on?
questions.why: The occipital condyles sit lateral to the foramen magnum and rest on the first vertebra of the spinal column.

options.why: That sits anteriorly in the cranial floor.
Those are on the temporal bones.
Those form the top of the cranium.

questions.stem: What shape is the sphenoid bone described as?
questions.why: The sphenoid is butterfly-shaped, sits anteriorly in the cranium, spans the width of the skull, and forms part of the cranial cavity floor.

options.why: That is not the description used.
That describes the hyoid bone.
That describes the lacrimal bones.

questions.stem: Which structure does the optic nerve pass through?
questions.why: The optic canal allows the optic nerve to reach the eye. The superior orbital fissure is a separate opening for the eye movement nerves.

options.why: That transmits the eye movement nerves.
That serves the chin and lower lip.
That transmits the spinal cord.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerves pass through the superior orbital fissure?
questions.why: The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV, and VI, which control eye movements.

options.why: Those serve the face and expression.
Those serve smell and vision by other routes.
Those serve the throat and neck.

questions.stem: How many bones make up each orbit?
questions.why: Each orbit is made of 7 bones — four facial and three cranial: maxilla, zygomatic, lacrimal, palatine, frontal, ethmoid, and sphenoid.

options.why: That undercounts by one.
That overcounts the contributing bones.
That undercounts the contributing bones.

questions.stem: What shape is the orbit described as?
questions.why: The orbit is a quadrangular pyramidal cavity in the upper face, surrounding the eye and providing structural protection.

options.why: The orbit tapers rather than being round.
It is a cavity rather than a canal.
It is deep rather than shallow.

questions.stem: How many bones make up the face?
questions.why: 14 bones make up the face, and 12 of them are paired, meaning there is a left and a right of each.

options.why: That overcounts the facial bones.
That is the cranial count.
That undercounts the facial bones.

questions.stem: Which facial bone does NOT join the maxillae?
questions.why: Two fused maxillary bones form the upper jaw, and all facial bones except the mandible join them.

options.why: It meets the maxilla at the nasal bridge.
The cheekbone articulates with the maxilla.
It forms part of the orbit alongside the maxilla.

questions.stem: What do the lacrimal bones house?
questions.why: Lacrimal bones are fingernail-sized, form part of the medial orbital walls, and house the tear ducts — lacrima means tear.

options.why: That runs through the ethmoid.
Those sit within the maxillae.
That is formed by the sphenoid.

questions.stem: What forms the lower part of the nose?
questions.why: The nasal bones form the bridge of the nose; the lower part of the nose is cartilage.

options.why: That contributes to the septum.
Those form the upper jaw.
That contributes to the septum and orbit.

questions.stem: What is unique about the mandible's joints?
questions.why: The mandible is the largest and strongest facial bone. It joins the temporal bones on each side, forming the only freely movable joints in the skull.

options.t: They are the only paired skull joints
options.why: Many skull structures are paired.

options.t: They are the only freely movable skull joints
They are the only cartilaginous skull joints
options.why: Skull joints are largely fibrous.

options.t: They are the only fused skull joints
options.why: Fused joints are the sutures elsewhere in the skull.

questions.stem: What passes through the mental foramen?
questions.why: The mental foramen allows blood vessels and the inferior alveolar nerve to reach the chin and lower lip.

options.t: The facial nerve to the muscles
options.why: That exits at a different point on the temporal bone.

options.t: The optic nerve to the eye
options.why: That runs through the optic canal.

options.t: The spinal cord to the brainstem
options.why: That passes through the foramen magnum.

options.t: Vessels and the inferior alveolar nerve

questions.stem: What makes the hyoid bone unique?
questions.why: The horseshoe-shaped hyoid is the only bone in the body that does not connect directly with any other bone. It sits about 2 cm above the larynx.

options.t: It is the only unpaired neck bone
options.why: Being unpaired is not what makes it unique.
It stops growing like other bones.

options.t: It is entirely cartilage in adults
options.why: It is a true bone, not cartilage.

options.t: It connects to no other bone

questions.stem: What does the hyoid bone serve as?
questions.why: The hyoid is a movable base for the tongue and an attachment point for the neck muscles that raise and lower the larynx during swallowing and speech.

options.why: The SCM attaches to the mastoid process.

options.t: A movable base for the tongue
A protective shield for the trachea
options.why: It sits above the larynx rather than shielding the trachea.

options.t: The anchor for the mandibular joint
options.why: That joint is formed with the temporal bone.

questions.stem: What do all sinuses do?
questions.why: All sinuses lighten the skull bones and amplify the sounds we make as we speak.

options.why: Facial muscles attach to bone directly.
CSF drains through separate venous sinuses.

options.t: Lighten the skull and amplify speech

options.why: That is the job of the nasal passages.

questions.stem: Which is the largest paranasal sinus?
questions.why: The maxillary sinus is the largest, sitting laterally and inferiorly and draining underneath the frontal sinus opening.

options.why: It sits above the eyes but is smaller.
Those lie deep behind the eyes.
Those are small hollow spaces behind the nose.

questions.stem: Where do the ethmoid sinuses typically cause pain?
questions.why: Ethmoid sinuses are hollow spaces in the bone behind the nose and cause pain around the top of the nose and the lower eyes.

options.t: Around the top of the nose and lower eyes

options.why: That pattern points to the maxillary sinus.
That pattern points to the frontal sinus.

options.t: At the back of the head
options.why: That pattern points to the sphenoidal sinus.

questions.stem: Where does the sternocleidomastoid insert?
questions.why: The SCM is paired and two-headed, arising from the sternum and the clavicle. The heads fuse before inserting into the mastoid process.

options.why: Those articulate with the first vertebra.
The clavicle is one of its origins, not its insertion.
Neck muscles attach there, but not the SCM's insertion.

questions.stem: What happens when both sternocleidomastoids contract together?
questions.why: Both SCMs contracting together flex the neck. If only one contracts, the head rotates toward the opposite shoulder.

options.why: Extension is the trapezius action.
Shoulder elevation is a trapezius action.
Rotation requires only one side to contract.

questions.stem: Which vessel runs superficial to the sternocleidomastoid?
questions.why: The external jugular runs superficially to the SCM, while the internal jugular and common carotid run deep to it — which is why the EJ is the accessible one.

options.why: That runs through the cervical vertebrae.
That runs deep to the muscle.
That also runs deep to the muscle.

questions.stem: To roughly which vertebral level does the trapezius extend?
questions.why: Each trapezius runs from the occipital bone down the vertebral column to approximately T12, inserting laterally on the scapular spine and clavicle.

options.why: That is in the lumbar spine.
That is at the base of the neck.
That is mid-thoracic, short of the full extent.

questions.stem: Which nerve innervates the trapezius?
questions.why: The trapezius extends the head, making it an antagonist of the sternocleidomastoid, and it is innervated by the accessory nerve.

options.why: That serves facial sensation and the jaw.
That serves the muscles of expression.
That serves the diaphragm.

questions.stem: How many cranial nerves are there?
questions.why: There are 12 paired cranial nerves connecting directly to the brain. The 31 pairs are the spinal nerves.

options.why: They are paired, not single.
That is the number of spinal nerve pairs.
That overstates the count.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve carries the sense of smell?
questions.why: The olfactory nerve (I) transmits sensory information about smells.

options.why: That carries vision.
That carries facial sensation.
That carries taste and facial movement.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve controls pupil size in response to light?
questions.why: The oculomotor nerve provides motor function to four of the six muscles around the eye and helps control pupil size as it responds to light.

options.why: That controls the superior oblique muscle.
That controls the lateral rectus muscle.
That carries the visual signal in, not the pupil response out.

questions.stem: Which muscle does the trochlear nerve control?
questions.why: The trochlear nerve (IV) controls the superior oblique muscle, producing downward, outward, and inward eye movements.

options.why: That is controlled by the oculomotor.
That is controlled by the abducens.
That is also controlled by the oculomotor.

questions.stem: Which is the largest cranial nerve?
questions.why: The trigeminal nerve (V) is the largest cranial nerve, with sensory and motor functions, divided into ophthalmic, maxillary, and mandibular branches.

options.why: That serves expression and taste.
That has the longest pathway but is not the largest.
That serves the neck muscles.

questions.stem: Which trigeminal division carries both sensory and motor fibers?
questions.why: Ophthalmic and maxillary divisions are sensory. The mandibular division carries both — sensation from ears, lower lip, and chin, plus motor control of the jaw.

options.why: That division is also sensory only.
Only one division carries motor fibers.
That division is sensory only.

questions.stem: Which muscle does the abducens nerve control?
questions.why: The abducens nerve (VI) controls the lateral rectus, moving the eye outward — the name matches the action, abduction.

options.why: That is also oculomotor territory.
That is controlled by the oculomotor.
That is the trochlear nerve's muscle.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve moves the muscles of facial expression?
questions.why: The facial nerve (VII) moves the muscles of expression, provides taste for most of the tongue, and supplies the salivary and tear glands.

options.why: That moves the neck muscles.
That moves the tongue.
That moves the jaw, not the expression muscles.

questions.stem: Which portion of cranial nerve VIII tracks head movement?
questions.why: The cochlear portion detects sound by loudness and pitch. The vestibular portion tracks linear and rotational head movement for balance.

options.why: That belongs to cranial nerve V.
That belongs to cranial nerve I.
That detects sound vibration.

questions.stem: Which part of the tongue does the glossopharyngeal nerve serve for taste?
questions.why: The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) provides taste for the back part of the tongue; the facial nerve covers most of the rest.

options.why: That is served by the facial nerve.
No single nerve serves only the tip.
Taste is divided among several nerves.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve has the longest pathway?
questions.why: The vagus nerve (X) originates in the medulla and extends from the head all the way into the abdomen.

options.why: That reaches only as far as the tongue.
That is the largest but stays in the head.
That reaches the neck and shoulders only.

questions.stem: Which function belongs to the vagus nerve?
questions.why: The vagus stimulates muscles of the chest and trunk organs including those driving peristalsis, and carries sensory information from the heart and intestines.

options.t: Controlling four of the six eye muscles
options.why: That is the oculomotor nerve.

options.t: Moving the muscles of the tongue
options.why: That is the hypoglossal nerve.
That is the accessory nerve.

options.t: Driving peristalsis in the digestive tract

questions.stem: Where does the spinal portion of the accessory nerve originate?
questions.why: The accessory nerve (XI) is a motor nerve controlling the neck muscles. Its spinal portion starts in the upper spinal cord and its cranial part in the medulla.

options.why: That is where its cranial portion begins.
No portion of it originates there.
No portion of it originates there.

questions.stem: What is the hypoglossal nerve responsible for?
questions.why: The hypoglossal nerve (XII) starts in the medulla oblongata and moves down into the jaw to control most of the tongue muscles.

options.why: That is the facial nerve.

options.t: Taste from the back of the tongue
options.why: That is the glossopharyngeal nerve.
That is the trigeminal nerve.

options.t: Moving most of the tongue muscles

questions.stem: Match each cranial nerve to its primary function.
questions.why: The three eye-movement nerves are III, IV, and VI. The vagus is the outlier that leaves the head entirely, which is why vagal stimulation affects heart rate and the gut.
pairs: Four of the six eye muscles plus pupil response
Largest cranial nerve; facial sensation and jaw movement
Longest pathway; sensation and motor control from throat to abdomen

questions.stem: Match each paranasal sinus to its location.
questions.why: Four paranasal sinuses, all of which lighten the skull and amplify speech. Maxillary is the largest and the one most often involved in sinus infection.
pairs: The largest; lateral and inferior, draining under the frontal sinus opening
Hollow spaces in the bone behind the nose
Two large cavities within the sphenoid bone behind the eyes

questions.stem: Match each bone to its defining feature.
questions.why: The cranium is 8 bones, the face is 14, and the hyoid belongs to neither group — it floats in the mid-neck, suspended by muscle.
pairs: Forms the forehead and the superior part of each orbit
Paired; forms most of the top and side walls of the cranium
Most posterior; contains the foramen magnum
Butterfly-shaped; forms part of the cranial cavity floor
Largest and strongest facial bone; only freely movable skull joints
The only bone connecting to no other bone
